name: Yabong
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Hodgkinson notes that in Masi, Bidua and Basor villages (Yabong language area) stress always occurs on the second syllable. No further statements can be made regarding stress, as it was not transcribed consistently.
new_statements.citation: Gray, Rachel, Hannah Paris, Daryl Pfantz, Dan Richardson & Juliann Bullock. 2015. A Sociolinguistic Survey of the Yabong [ybo], Migum [klm], Nekgini [nkg], and Neko [nej]. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2015-005. Dallas: SIL International.
new_statements.locator: Section 4.3 'Characteristics of the language', p. 38 (PDF p. 43)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (born-digital SIL PDF, 103 pp., Acrobat PDFMaker from Word). extracted text of PDF p. 43 (printed p. 38) gives the passage exactly as quoted: "Hodgkinson notes that in Masi, Bidua and Basor villages (Yabong language area) stress always occurs on the second syllable. No further statements can be made regarding stress, as it was not transcribed consistently." It is the closing paragraph of sec. 4.3 'Characteristics of the language' (consonant and vowel inventories, vowel clusters, SOV order, verb suffixes, negation) and the only prosodic remark in the report (grep for stress/accent/tone/pitch: no other hits). The abstract names Barbara Hodgkinson as a fieldwork member of the March 2008…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the second syllable of the word, as observed by the survey's wordlist transcriber (Barbara Hodgkinson) in three of the five Yabong villages (Masi, Bidua, Basor); the report itself cautions that stress was not transcribed consistently, so the observation is impressionistic and not backed by marked data.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the report says 'always', but immediately adds that no further statements can be made because stress was not transcribed consistently. Nothing said about monosyllables, the other Yabong villages (Gogu, Baded), or phrase-level effects.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word in isolation (SIL-PNG 190-item wordlist elicitation, citation forms, group elicitation in Tok Pisin). This is a one-sentence field observation in a sociolinguistic survey report, not a phonological analysis; the survey wordlists in Appendix A carry no stress marks. Hodgkinson was a member of the 2008 survey team (named in the abstract) but is not among the report's authors, so the statement is her observation as relayed by her co-workers in the same project.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement covers the Yabong language area proper (Masi, Bidua, Basor villages; Yabong = yabo1240, ISO ybo, Z'graggen's B11 in the Yaganon Family). Claassen & McElhanon 1970 and Gray et al. 2015 report only slight dialect variation among Yabong villages. Not to be confused with sibling Yaganon languages Saep (saep1240; its SIL OPD says stress tends to fall on the last root syllable and is subordinate to length), Ganglau or Dumun.

sources.note: Sec. 4.3 'Characteristics of the language', printed p. 38 (PDF p. 43): stress always on the second syllable in Masi, Bidua and Basor (Yabong area) per Barbara Hodgkinson, who elicited and transcribed the 190-item wordlists in March 2008; report adds that stress was not transcribed consistently so nothing further can be said. Appendix A Yabong wordlists carry no stress marks. Copy taken from the neko1240 audit folder (fetched sources there 2026-09-17; live SIL site is Cloudflare-walled).

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J. A. 1980. A comparative word list of the Rai Coast languages, Madang Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-30. Canberra: ANU. xv+181 pp.
sources.note: Yabong is language B11 (Yaganon Family); wordlist columns only. Introduction discusses pronouns, possession, negation; no mention of stress, accent, tone, pitch or suprasegmentals (grep of full text layer).

sources.note: Classification and lexicostatistics; Yabong appears only in tables; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur (extracted text grep). Silent.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11 (Pacific Linguistics A-23), 45-78.
sources.note: Sec. 3.4.1 Yabong (pop. 310, five villages west of the Yangda River; lists from Gogou, Bidua, Basor). Sec. 6.1.1 'Phonology' for the Yaganon languages covers consonants only (prenasalised stops word-initially in Yabong; flap vs lateral). 'Stress', 'accent', 'tone' do not occur anywhere in the paper. Silent.
